newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Thousands protest Bulgarian govt economic policies.
newsitem.headline: Thousands protest Bulgarian govt economic policies.

text.p: Thousands of Bulgarians gathered in front of Sofia's gilded Orthodox cathedral on Tuesday to denounce the Socialist government's economic management less than two weeks before presidential elections.
Church bells tolled in the background as protesters chanting "Resign, resign" set fire to electricity bills inflated by the collapse of the national currency.

"Bulgaria was never in its history in such a deep economic crisis and its population was never poorer than now," Konstantin Trenchev, head of independent trade union Podkrepa, told the early evening rally.

Monthly inflation is nearing 20 percent and power and bread shortages loom during the coming Balkan winter. The International Monetary Fund has delayed a badly-needed $115 million credit because of the slow pace of economic reform.
"All the bright and educated people are fleeing the country because here they have no future...look at the crowds in front of the embassies and consular services," said Trenchev.
Voters' minds are more on the economic crisis than the low-key campaign for the October 27 election.
Under its post-communist constitution, Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic in which the president is a largely ceremonial figure with limited powers.
Most political power is held by parliament where the Socialist Party, composed largely of former communists, has a majority.
"Humiliation and poverty brought us here this evening," Zhivka Petrova, a worker in a military plant, told the crowd.

"In the past six months, bread prices shot up by 150 percent, milk by 130 percent, while our income has dropped by 38 percent. Basic foods like bread and milk have become a luxury for us...not to mention electricity and heating."
Bulgaria's biggest trade union organisation, the Independent Labour Confederation, has called a one-day general strike for November 20.
Senior politicians of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces did not attend the rally but demonstrators waved blue UDF banners as well as purple Podkrepa flags.

Police stepped up security before the rally in response to a war of words between the unions and the government but police presence at the event itself was light and demonstrators dispersed afterwards without incident.
Socialist party spokeswoman Klara Marinova criticised the timing of the rally so soon before the elections. "All problems can be solved only through negotiation, not in the city's squares," she said.
